The Work, Leadership and Torah Teaching of Rav Huna: The Pillar of the Second Generation of the Babylonian Amoraim
Introduction and Chronological Distinction in Talmudic and Geonic Literature
Historical and Talmudic scholarship must make a careful and thorough distinction between different persons who bear identical names in rabbinic literature and in the epistles of the Geonim, in order to avoid anachronism and errors in identifying the sources.[1] The central figure of Rav Huna, the renowned Babylonian Amora of the second generation, is sometimes interwoven in halakhic literature with earlier or later figures who were active in the Babylonian sphere.[1, 2] Rav Huna's name is mentioned hundreds of times in the Babylonian Talmud and the Jerusalem Talmud, a fact that attests to his undisputed centrality in shaping the halakha and the public leadership of his generation.[2] To clarify the political and halakhic background of his activity, a clear distinction must be drawn between three key figures who bear the name "Huna":
Rav Huna the Amora was born in the town of Drukeret in Babylonia in the first half of the third century CE, his estimated year of birth being 3976, the year 214–215 CE, or the year 528 of the Seleucid era (minyan shtarot).[2, 4] His father was Natan, and he must not be confused with the later Amora Rav Huna son of Rav Natan, who lived several generations after him and was active at the end of the days of Rav Ashi.[4, 6] According to the chronological tradition, Rav Huna was a descendant of the family of the Exilarch, and he may have been the direct grandson of Rav Huna I, the first Exilarch mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud.[2, 4] This aristocratic lineage gave him a built-in closeness to the house of the Exilarch of his generation, and profoundly influenced the mutual relationship between the world of Torah and the political and autonomous leadership of Babylonian Jewry.[2, 4]
The Biographical Path: From Extreme Poverty to Great Wealth and Works of Kindness
Rav Huna's life was marked by a dramatic swing from severe economic hardship in his youth to prosperity and great wealth in his old age.[4, 7] During the period of his studies with Rav and with Shmuel, Rav Huna was desperately poor and made a meager living from physical work in agriculture, including plowing, irrigating fields and herding animals.[2, 4, 7] The Talmudic sources describe how one Sabbath he had no wine for Kiddush and Havdalah, and so he was forced to pawn his belt, his personal girdle, to tie a rope in its place, and to appear thus in the study hall of Rav.[2, 4, 7] When his teacher asked him the meaning of the rope, he told him of his distress, and Rav blessed him that he would attain wealth so great that he would be able to go about in garments of silk and velvet.[7]
Over the years Rav's blessing was fulfilled in full.[7] Rav Huna began to trade in wine, his business prospered and he became exceedingly wealthy.[4, 7] Nevertheless, his commercial success was accompanied by incisive moral tests that shaped his public character.[4] The Talmud relates that four hundred barrels of wine in his possession turned sour, and the sages suggested that he examine his deeds.[4, 8] When he asked whether he was suspect in their eyes of doing wrong, they answered him that the Holy One, blessed be He, is not suspect of executing judgment without justice.[8] On inquiry it emerged that Rav Huna had refrained from paying his sharecropper the share of the vine shoots due to him, because the sharecropper used to steal regularly from Rav Huna's portion.[4] The sages held that although the sharecropper stole, Rav Huna should not take the law into his own hands, for even one who steals from a thief tastes the taste of theft.[4] Rav Huna accepted their words and returned the payment to the sharecropper, and the soured wine turned back into fine wine, or was sold at the price of expensive vinegar.[4, 8]
Rav Huna's great wealth was translated into a wide-ranging philanthropic and public enterprise that combined practical care for the weak with the preservation of the local economy.[2, 4] On winter days Rav Huna was carried in a magnificent golden chair, a "guharka de-dahava," intended for the notables of the city, and inspected the condition of the houses in the city.[2, 4] He ordered every dilapidated building that posed a danger to the public to be demolished; if the owner of the house was poor and could not rebuild it, Rav Huna financed the construction from his private funds.[2, 4] In addition, he made a point of buying up all the surplus goods of the vegetable sellers in the market toward the end of the day, in order to prevent them from suffering losses that would deter them from bringing goods to the city.[2, 4] His house was always open to host the needy, and before every meal he would proclaim: whoever is hungry, let him come and eat.[2, 4]
In his personal life Rav Huna experienced complex family tragedies.[2] His wife Chova bore him sons and daughters, but because of the resentment of his close colleague Rav Ada bar Ahava over the fact that Chova cut her children's hair in a "rounding of the head" haircut – an act that Rav Ada regarded as a Torah prohibition, whereas she regarded her sons as exempt – all his sons died in childhood.[2] Only after the death of Rav Ada was his famous son, the Amora Rabbah bar Rav Huna, born to him.[2] Rav Huna educated his son in good character traits and self-control, and even tested his anger in a controlled manner by tearing an expensive silk garment in his presence.[2] His wife Chova outlived him, and Rav Nachman treated her with great honor in accordance with the rule "the wife of a colleague is like a colleague."[2] Rav Huna also possessed applied medical knowledge, and his compound remedy for cough and consumption – based on ash from seven ovens and hairs from the beard of an old dog – is brought in the Talmud as a folk medical tradition.[2]
Institutional Leadership and the Headship of the Sura Yeshiva
After the death of Rav, the founder of the Sura yeshiva, the Torah center in Babylonia went through a complex interim period.[7, 9] For seven years a group of Torah scholars was active in Sura without an official head of the yeshiva, out of respect for the Amora Shmuel, who was active in Nehardea and was the leading halakhic authority.[7, 9] After the death of Shmuel, the sages of Babylonia deliberated for three years on the question of the appointment.[7] Three options stood before them: Rav Huna, who was thirty-seven years old and close to the Exilarch; Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, who was one of the most important students of Rav; or Rav Yehuda, who was older than Rav Huna.[7] In the end it was decided to appoint Rav Huna head of the Sura yeshiva, a post he held for about forty years, and he was the first to be called by the official title "Rosh Yeshiva" (head of the yeshiva).[2, 9]
Under Rav Huna's leadership the Sura yeshiva enjoyed unprecedented demographic and Torah flourishing.[2] The number of regular students in the yeshiva reached eight hundred, and in his public discourses he was assisted by thirteen Amoraim who conveyed his words aloud to the crowds.[2, 10] The intensity of the attendance at the yeshiva is described vividly in the Talmud: when the listeners stood up at the end of the discourse and shook the dust from their garments, a cloud of dust rose so great that it darkened the sun, and the darkness was felt as far as the Land of Israel, where they knew to say that Rav Huna's lesson had ended.[2, 10]
The lessons in the yeshiva were extremely long and demanding.[2] Sixty of the greatest sages, among them Rav Giddel, Rabbi Chelbo, Rav Sheshet and Rav Acha bar Yaakov, fell ill and were physically harmed because they held themselves back for a long time from going out to relieve themselves during the lengthy discourses.[2, 10] It is told of Rav Acha bar Yaakov that he was suspended from the cedar of the study hall in order to be freed of his illness, and he declared that of the sixty elders who were harmed only he was saved, by virtue of the verse "Wisdom preserves the life of those who have it."[10]
Despite his absolute authority, Rav Huna displayed extraordinary gentleness of spirit in his attitude toward his students.[2] He refused to use them for personal tasks that they were not accustomed to perform in their own towns, so as not to demean them.[2, 7, 10] Thus, for example, when he was returning from the field with a hoe on his shoulder and met the sage Rav Huna bar Chanilai, who asked to carry the implement for him, Rav Huna refused, saying: "If you are accustomed to carry such implements in your town – I will give it to you; but if not, I do not wish to be honored through your disgrace."[7]
Rav Huna's public authority extended beyond the borders of Babylonia, and he was recognized as the greatest of the generation even in the Land of Israel.[2] Rabbi Assi defined him as "the head of the heads of the tribes," whose status as an "expert individual" allows him to release vows on his own.[2] Because of his exalted Torah standing, he was permitted to be called up first to the Torah in the synagogue in place of the priests, and even Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, the most senior priests in the Land of Israel, were subject to his halakhic authority.[2, 10] This was in contrast to Rav, who was not called up first to the Torah because Shmuel, a priest, was present and led the congregation.[10]
The Dialectic of Master and Student: The Relationship with Rav Chisda
The relationship between Rav Huna and the greatest of his students, Rav Chisda, presents a complex dialectical bond that moved between relations of absolute subordination and scholarly partnership and incisive mutual criticism.[2, 11] The two, who were called together by the titles "the elders of Sura" and "the pious men of Babylonia," conducted an extensive halakhic give-and-take characterized by enormous esteem alongside disputes of principle.[2, 11] Rav Chisda displayed supreme respect toward his teacher; as long as Rav Huna was alive, Rav Chisda refused to issue halakhic rulings in Sura even on the simplest questions, so as not to impinge on the exclusive halakhic authority of his teacher.[2] Rav Huna for his part greatly appreciated Rav Chisda's wisdom, called his words "gracious and fine," and even rebuked his son Rabbah, who avoided studying with Rav Chisda because of his engagement in health and medical guidance.[2]
Nevertheless, the scholarly and personal tension between the two reached its peak in a famous confrontation in the course of the discussion of the laws of returning a lost object.[12, 13] Rav Chisda asked Rav Huna: "A student whom his teacher needs – what [is the law]?"[10, 13] The question dealt with a situation in which the teacher needs the knowledge of the student, who has heard traditions from other sages: does the teacher's lost object still take precedence over the father's lost object?[12, 13] Rav Huna interpreted the question as a personal provocation and an attempt to hint that he needed Rav Chisda's learning, or to hint at his poor economic situation in the past, when he had needed help, and answered sharply: "Chisda, Chisda, I do not need you; you will need me for forty years."[10, 12, 13] This confrontation led to a prolonged estrangement, and because of the distress and the mutual suspicion the two sages sat and fasted forty fasts each.[10, 13]
Another substantive dispute between the two, as the scholar Geoffrey Herman notes, concerned the attitude toward the institution of the Exilarch and his political and halakhic standing.[4] Rav Huna, who was a descendant of the Exilarch's family, maintained a close relationship and mutual esteem with the house of the Exilarch, and tended to grant them distinctive halakhic leniencies.[2, 4] Thus, for example, he permitted the Exilarch's wife to go out on the Sabbath into the public domain wearing an expensive "city of gold" ornament, despite the general prohibition the Sages decreed out of concern that she might take off the ornament to show it to her friends.[2] By contrast, Rav Chisda's attitude toward the Exilarch was highly critical and negative.[4] This was also expressed in their dispute recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud as to whether it is permitted to carry the Exilarch on a chair from place to place on the festivals of Israel, where Rav Huna tended to be lenient in deference to the Exilarch's honor, whereas Rav Chisda was stringent and regarded it as a weekday activity (uvdin de-chol).[4] Four years before Rav Huna's death, Rav Chisda established an independent study hall of his own in Sura, a step that expresses his growing halakhic independence in the last days of his teacher.[2]
Halakhic and Legal Rulings
As a judge and head of the yeshiva, Rav Huna ran a firm and activist legal system that enjoyed official backing from the Exilarch.[2] He used this authority to punish serious offenders and even ordered the cutting off of the hand of a violent man who regularly struck others.[2] These rulings attest to the Babylonian legal approach, which judges according to the circumstances existing on the ground and the need for social deterrence.[2]
Within the laws of commerce and the prevention of interest, Rav Huna also discussed the law of fixing the prices of produce before the market price is published, in order to prevent the violation of the prohibition of interest in future transactions.[4] His rulings reflect a combination of strictness in monetary law together with practical solutions that take into account the needs of the market and the local economy in Babylonia.[4]
The World of Thought, Ethics and Theology
Rav Huna's theological and moral thought reflects a deep social and existential approach that firmly rejects detached scholarship and places social responsibility at the center of the service of God.[4, 15] This principle is formulated in his famous saying in Tractate Avodah Zarah: "Whoever engages in Torah alone is like one who has no God."[2, 4, 15] This saying serves as the key to understanding the story of the arrest of Rabbi Elazar ben Perata and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon by the Romans.[15] Rabbi Chanina wondered why he had been sentenced to be burned in fire together with the Torah scroll while Rabbi Elazar was saved, and Rabbi Elazar answered him that he had engaged both in Torah and in acts of kindness, whereas Rabbi Chanina had engaged in Torah alone.[15] The Gemara raises a difficulty and notes that Rabbi Chanina was a faithful charity collector, but clarifies that managing charity funds is not equivalent to physical and personal acts of kindness, in accordance with the principle Rav Huna laid down.[15, 16] Torah without inner and practical kindness is perceived as spiritual idolatry, devoid of true divine presence.[15, 16]
Alongside his social commitment, Rav Huna was characterized by deep religious and existential sensitivity.[12] The Talmud relates that when he reached verses expressing distance and loss of connection between man and his God, such as the obligation of appearing at the Temple, he would weep.[12] He would ask in pain: "A servant whose master longs to see him – shall he be kept far from him? A servant whose master longs to eat at his table – shall he be kept far from him?"[12] These questions express the sense of spiritual orphanhood that the Amoraim felt after the destruction of the Temple, and Rav Huna's infinite yearning for unmediated closeness to God.[12]
His conception of the world of prayer is based on stability and inner fear of Heaven [17]:
Fixing a place for prayer: Rav Huna established that "whoever fixes a place for his prayer – the God of Abraham is his help, and when he dies they say of him: Alas, the humble one! Alas, the pious one! Of the disciples of Abraham our father."[17] The fixedness is not merely technical, but attests to submission, humility and concentration of the soul, which connect the one who prays to the historical chain of the patriarchs.[17]
The Minchah prayer: Rav Huna emphasized the special importance of the Minchah (afternoon) prayer, noting that Elijah the prophet was answered on Mount Carmel only at the time of the Minchah prayer, which represents the halting of the flow of the day's work in order to stand before the Creator.[17]
Fear of Heaven as the key to influence: Rav Huna taught that "every person who has fear of Heaven – his words are heeded," out of the understanding that a leader's authority does not stem from his public power but from his religious and moral integrity, which radiates onto his surroundings and leads to the willing acceptance of his rulings.[17]
The resting of the Divine Presence in exile: Rabbi Abba testified to his personal holiness in his eulogy for him: "Our master was worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon him, but Babylonia prevented it."[10] The geographical space of the Babylonian exile was perceived as a factor preventing the full revelation of prophecy, despite Rav Huna's supreme spiritual level.[10]
His Last Days and His Influence on the Generations
Rav Huna lived a long life and died suddenly in 297 CE, at over the age of eighty.[2, 4] His sudden death at first aroused concern among the sages of Babylonia that this was a "snatched death," indicating a hidden sin.[2] However, sages from the town of Mehadeyav clarified that a sudden death above the age of eighty is considered an honored and prestigious "death by a kiss," reserved for the perfectly righteous.[2] Rav Chisda conducted his funeral procession according to laws he had heard from Rav Huna himself, and in accordance with his will his bones were taken up to the Land of Israel.[2] He was buried in the burial cave of the Tanna Rabbi Chiyya and his sons in Tiberias, alongside the great ones of the nation.[1, 2, 4]
With the death of Rav Huna, an organizational change took place in the centers of Torah in Babylonia.[11] At first the supreme Torah leadership passed to the Pumbedita yeshiva under the headship of his colleague Rav Yehuda, but this situation lasted only about two years, until the death of Rav Yehuda in 299 CE.[11] After that the institutional primacy returned to the Sura yeshiva, when Rav Chisda was appointed its third head at the age of 82.[11] Rav Chisda led Sura for ten years until his death in 309 CE, and after him study continued under the unofficial leadership of Rav Huna's son, Rabbah bar Rav Huna, until about the year 322 CE.[11, 18] The Sura yeshiva went through periods of decline and temporary closure, until it was reopened in the glorious era of Rav Ashi.[11, 18]
Rav Huna's work and teaching shaped the image of the ideal spiritual leader in Babylonia.[2, 4] The fascinating combination of extremes – between degrading poverty and noble wealth, between judicial firmness and public humility, and between outstanding scholarship and deep social commitment – made him a model to be emulated by later generations.[2, 4, 7] Evidence of his long-term influence is found in the prayer of the later Amora Rava, who prayed to attain the complete and comprehensive wisdom of Rav Huna, a wisdom that fused Torah, leadership and social justice into a single inseparable entity.[2]

This text surveys the multifaceted figure of Rav Huna, the central leader of the second generation of the Babylonian Amoraim and head of the Sura yeshiva, while distinguishing between him and other persons bearing an identical name. The article outlines his unique life path, which moved from extreme poverty in his youth to great wealth that was used for wide-ranging works of kindness and care for the public welfare. On the level of leadership, the text emphasizes the Torah flourishing of the Sura yeshiva under his exclusive authority, alongside the complex and dialectical relationship he conducted with his foremost student Rav Chisda. Finally, the source presents his moral and theological teaching, which weaves together deep scholarship with social responsibility and fear of Heaven, and fortifies his standing as the pillar of Babylonian Jewry through the generations.

Under Rav Huna's leadership the Sura yeshiva enjoyed unprecedented demographic and Torah flourishing.[2] The number of regular students in the yeshiva reached eight hundred, and in his public discourses he was assisted by thirteen Amoraim who conveyed his words aloud to the crowds.[2, 10] The intensity of the attendance at the yeshiva is described vividly in the Talmud: when the listeners stood up at the end of the discourse and shook the dust from their garments, a cloud of dust rose so great that it darkened the sun, and the darkness was felt as far as the Land of Israel, where they knew to say that Rav Huna's lesson had ended.[2, 10]
The lessons in the yeshiva were extremely long and demanding.[2] Sixty of the greatest sages, among them Rav Giddel, Rabbi Chelbo, Rav Sheshet and Rav Acha bar Yaakov, fell ill and were physically harmed because they held themselves back for a long time from going out to relieve themselves during the lengthy discourses.[2, 10] It is told of Rav Acha bar Yaakov that he was suspended from the cedar of the study hall in order to be freed of his illness, and he declared that of the sixty elders who were harmed only he was saved, by virtue of the verse "Wisdom preserves the life of those who have it."[10]
Despite his absolute authority, Rav Huna displayed extraordinary gentleness of spirit in his attitude toward his students.[2] He refused to use them for personal tasks that they were not accustomed to perform in their own towns, so as not to demean them.[2, 7, 10] Thus, for example, when he was returning from the field with a hoe on his shoulder and met the sage Rav Huna bar Chanilai, who asked to carry the implement for him, Rav Huna refused, saying: "If you are accustomed to carry such implements in your town – I will give it to you; but if not, I do not wish to be honored through your disgrace."[7]
Rav Huna's public authority extended beyond the borders of Babylonia, and he was recognized as the greatest of the generation even in the Land of Israel.[2] Rabbi Assi defined him as "the head of the heads of the tribes," whose status as an "expert individual" allows him to release vows on his own.[2] Because of his exalted Torah standing, he was permitted to be called up first to the Torah in the synagogue in place of the priests, and even Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, the most senior priests in the Land of Israel, were subject to his halakhic authority.[2, 10] This was in contrast to Rav, who was not called up first to the Torah because Shmuel, a priest, was present and led the congregation.[10]
The Dialectic of Master and Student: The Relationship with Rav Chisda
The relationship between Rav Huna and the greatest of his students, Rav Chisda, presents a complex dialectical bond that moved between relations of absolute subordination and scholarly partnership and incisive mutual criticism.[2, 11] The two, who were called together by the titles "the elders of Sura" and "the pious men of Babylonia," conducted an extensive halakhic give-and-take characterized by enormous esteem alongside disputes of principle.[2, 11] Rav Chisda displayed supreme respect toward his teacher; as long as Rav Huna was alive, Rav Chisda refused to issue halakhic rulings in Sura even on the simplest questions, so as not to impinge on the exclusive halakhic authority of his teacher.[2] Rav Huna for his part greatly appreciated Rav Chisda's wisdom, called his words "gracious and fine," and even rebuked his son Rabbah, who avoided studying with Rav Chisda because of his engagement in health and medical guidance.[2]
Nevertheless, the scholarly and personal tension between the two reached its peak in a famous confrontation in the course of the discussion of the laws of returning a lost object.[12, 13] Rav Chisda asked Rav Huna: "A student whom his teacher needs – what [is the law]?"[10, 13] The question dealt with a situation in which the teacher needs the knowledge of the student, who has heard traditions from other sages: does the teacher's lost object still take precedence over the father's lost object?[12, 13] Rav Huna interpreted the question as a personal provocation and an attempt to hint that he needed Rav Chisda's learning, or to hint at his poor economic situation in the past, when he had needed help, and answered sharply: "Chisda, Chisda, I do not need you; you will need me for forty years."[10, 12, 13] This confrontation led to a prolonged estrangement, and because of the distress and the mutual suspicion the two sages sat and fasted forty fasts each.[10, 13]
Another substantive dispute between the two, as the scholar Geoffrey Herman notes, concerned the attitude toward the institution of the Exilarch and his political and halakhic standing.[4] Rav Huna, who was a descendant of the Exilarch's family, maintained a close relationship and mutual esteem with the house of the Exilarch, and tended to grant them distinctive halakhic leniencies.[2, 4] Thus, for example, he permitted the Exilarch's wife to go out on the Sabbath into the public domain wearing an expensive "city of gold" ornament, despite the general prohibition the Sages decreed out of concern that she might take off the ornament to show it to her friends.[2] By contrast, Rav Chisda's attitude toward the Exilarch was highly critical and negative.[4] This was also expressed in their dispute recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud as to whether it is permitted to carry the Exilarch on a chair from place to place on the festivals of Israel, where Rav Huna tended to be lenient in deference to the Exilarch's honor, whereas Rav Chisda was stringent and regarded it as a weekday activity (uvdin de-chol).[4] Four years before Rav Huna's death, Rav Chisda established an independent study hall of his own in Sura, a step that expresses his growing halakhic independence in the last days of his teacher.[2]
Halakhic and Legal Rulings
As a judge and head of the yeshiva, Rav Huna ran a firm and activist legal system that enjoyed official backing from the Exilarch.[2] He used this authority to punish serious offenders and even ordered the cutting off of the hand of a violent man who regularly struck others.[2] These rulings attest to the Babylonian legal approach, which judges according to the circumstances existing on the ground and the need for social deterrence.[2]
Within the laws of commerce and the prevention of interest, Rav Huna also discussed the law of fixing the prices of produce before the market price is published, in order to prevent the violation of the prohibition of interest in future transactions.[4] His rulings reflect a combination of strictness in monetary law together with practical solutions that take into account the needs of the market and the local economy in Babylonia.[4]
The World of Thought, Ethics and Theology
Rav Huna's theological and moral thought reflects a deep social and existential approach that firmly rejects detached scholarship and places social responsibility at the center of the service of God.[4, 15] This principle is formulated in his famous saying in Tractate Avodah Zarah: "Whoever engages in Torah alone is like one who has no God."[2, 4, 15] This saying serves as the key to understanding the story of the arrest of Rabbi Elazar ben Perata and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon by the Romans.[15] Rabbi Chanina wondered why he had been sentenced to be burned in fire together with the Torah scroll while Rabbi Elazar was saved, and Rabbi Elazar answered him that he had engaged both in Torah and in acts of kindness, whereas Rabbi Chanina had engaged in Torah alone.[15] The Gemara raises a difficulty and notes that Rabbi Chanina was a faithful charity collector, but clarifies that managing charity funds is not equivalent to physical and personal acts of kindness, in accordance with the principle Rav Huna laid down.[15, 16] Torah without inner and practical kindness is perceived as spiritual idolatry, devoid of true divine presence.[15, 16]
Alongside his social commitment, Rav Huna was characterized by deep religious and existential sensitivity.[12] The Talmud relates that when he reached verses expressing distance and loss of connection between man and his God, such as the obligation of appearing at the Temple, he would weep.[12] He would ask in pain: "A servant whose master longs to see him – shall he be kept far from him? A servant whose master longs to eat at his table – shall he be kept far from him?"[12] These questions express the sense of spiritual orphanhood that the Amoraim felt after the destruction of the Temple, and Rav Huna's infinite yearning for unmediated closeness to God.[12]
His conception of the world of prayer is based on stability and inner fear of Heaven [17]:
Fixing a place for prayer: Rav Huna established that "whoever fixes a place for his prayer – the God of Abraham is his help, and when he dies they say of him: Alas, the humble one! Alas, the pious one! Of the disciples of Abraham our father."[17] The fixedness is not merely technical, but attests to submission, humility and concentration of the soul, which connect the one who prays to the historical chain of the patriarchs.[17]
The Minchah prayer: Rav Huna emphasized the special importance of the Minchah (afternoon) prayer, noting that Elijah the prophet was answered on Mount Carmel only at the time of the Minchah prayer, which represents the halting of the flow of the day's work in order to stand before the Creator.[17]
Fear of Heaven as the key to influence: Rav Huna taught that "every person who has fear of Heaven – his words are heeded," out of the understanding that a leader's authority does not stem from his public power but from his religious and moral integrity, which radiates onto his surroundings and leads to the willing acceptance of his rulings.[17]
The resting of the Divine Presence in exile: Rabbi Abba testified to his personal holiness in his eulogy for him: "Our master was worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon him, but Babylonia prevented it."[10] The geographical space of the Babylonian exile was perceived as a factor preventing the full revelation of prophecy, despite Rav Huna's supreme spiritual level.[10]
His Last Days and His Influence on the Generations
Rav Huna lived a long life and died suddenly in 297 CE, at over the age of eighty.[2, 4] His sudden death at first aroused concern among the sages of Babylonia that this was a "snatched death," indicating a hidden sin.[2] However, sages from the town of Mehadeyav clarified that a sudden death above the age of eighty is considered an honored and prestigious "death by a kiss," reserved for the perfectly righteous.[2] Rav Chisda conducted his funeral procession according to laws he had heard from Rav Huna himself, and in accordance with his will his bones were taken up to the Land of Israel.[2] He was buried in the burial cave of the Tanna Rabbi Chiyya and his sons in Tiberias, alongside the great ones of the nation.[1, 2, 4]
With the death of Rav Huna, an organizational change took place in the centers of Torah in Babylonia.[11] At first the supreme Torah leadership passed to the Pumbedita yeshiva under the headship of his colleague Rav Yehuda, but this situation lasted only about two years, until the death of Rav Yehuda in 299 CE.[11] After that the institutional primacy returned to the Sura yeshiva, when Rav Chisda was appointed its third head at the age of 82.[11] Rav Chisda led Sura for ten years until his death in 309 CE, and after him study continued under the unofficial leadership of Rav Huna's son, Rabbah bar Rav Huna, until about the year 322 CE.[11, 18] The Sura yeshiva went through periods of decline and temporary closure, until it was reopened in the glorious era of Rav Ashi.[11, 18]
Rav Huna's work and teaching shaped the image of the ideal spiritual leader in Babylonia.[2, 4] The fascinating combination of extremes – between degrading poverty and noble wealth, between judicial firmness and public humility, and between outstanding scholarship and deep social commitment – made him a model to be emulated by later generations.[2, 4, 7] Evidence of his long-term influence is found in the prayer of the later Amora Rava, who prayed to attain the complete and comprehensive wisdom of Rav Huna, a wisdom that fused Torah, leadership and social justice into a single inseparable entity.[2]
